question: Loki, Moe, Nick and Ott are good friends. Ott had no money, but the others did. Moe gave Ott one-fifth of his money, Loki gave Ott one-fourth of his money and Nick gave Ott one-third of his money. Each gave Ott the same amount of money. What fractional part of the group’s money does Ott now have?
solution:
Because the three gifts are equal, use the common positive gift as one unit of money. Moe gave one-fifth of his money, so he originally had \(5\) such units. Similarly, Loki originally had \(4\) units and Nick had \(3\) units. Ott started with none, so the group's total was
\[
5+4+3=12\text{ units}.
\]
The gifts transfer money within the group, leaving this total unchanged. Ott now has the three gifted units, so his fraction of the group's money is
\[
\frac{3}{12}=\frac14,
\]
choice \(\text{B}\).

nodes.description: Solve real world problems involving division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and division of whole numbers by unit fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction model s and equations to represent the problem. For example, how much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 1/3-cup servings are in 2 cups of raisins?
nodes.label: 5.NF.B.7c

nodes.description: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions , and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. For example, create a story context for (2/3) ÷ (3/4) and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient; use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (2/3) ÷ (3/4) = 8/9 because 3/4 of 8/9 is 2/3. (In general, (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc.) How much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 3/4-cup servings are in 2/3 of a cup of yogurt? How wide is a rectangular strip of land with length 3/4 mi and area 1/2 square mi?
nodes.label: 6.NS.A.1

nodes.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem. For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.

edges.reason: Division introduces equal sharing, a useful conceptual bridge. Folding one whole into equal paper parts establishes a unit fraction without division notation or the inverse-multiplication interpretation.
A general fraction takes several equal unit parts; one such part is the unit-fraction concept directly contained in that construction.
edges.scope: fraction as a count of unit fractional parts

edges.reason: The criteria expressly find common factors and reduce until numerator and denominator are coprime. These are the common-factor contents of the endpoint; finding the greatest factor in a single step is only a shortcut and is outside this required scope.
edges.scope: Finding a shared divisor and recognizing the absence of a shared divisor above one when reducing to simplest form

edges.reason: Reduction replaces numerator and denominator by division by the same common factor, using the value-preserving fraction property.
edges.scope: dividing numerator and denominator by a common number

edges.reason: The unit-whole criterion interprets a fractional part of the whole and then inverts that relation. Fraction-of-a-quantity modeling is necessary, without requiring the endpoint's preferred arithmetic implementation.
edges.scope: identifying the unit whole in the fraction relation

edges.reason: The target writes and evaluates a fractional division expression, containing the division-by-fraction operation.
